title: SDK handoff latency budgeting and structured telemetry — PRD draft
content:
Overview:
This doc sketches a product requirement draft for a cohesive set of Hosted API features that center on three tightly-coupled concerns: (1) explicit SDK handoff semantics for tool-calling and partial responses, (2) runtime latency budgeting so clients and servers can make coordinated trade-offs, and (3) a small, intentionally-designed structured telemetry surface to make end-to-end latency/cost/safety trade-offs observable and automatable.

Context and motivation:
We continue to iterate on streaming + tool-calling UX, but two recurring pain points surface in customer interviews and internal debugging: ambiguous client expectations during partial/interruptible responses, and lack of consistent telemetry that ties a generated token sequence to downstream tool calls and SDK retries. Engineers build ad-hoc heuristics (client-side timers, exponential backoff, repeated retries) and operators struggle to reason about where latency/cost is incurred (model time vs tool call vs network vs SDK shim).

Problem statement (concise):
- When hosted API streams an incremental response that includes tool-handshake frames, clients currently lack a robust way to express how much latency they can tolerate at each stage (generation vs tool execution) and how they expect the SDK to behave on timeout or partial tool failure.
- Platform/ops cannot reliably attribute token-level latency to tool calls and SDK adapters because telemetry is fragmented between HTTP logs, model traces, and client-side metrics.

Goals (what success looks like):
1) Define an SDK-level contract that specifies: latency budget, retry strategy, and partial-result semantics for tool calls surfaced inside a stream. SDKs should expose simple defaults for typical web/mobile use cases and allow advanced tuning.
2) Introduce a compact telemetry schema (server + SDK) linking generation frames to tool call attempts and their outcomes with minimal overhead.
3) Provide server-side enforcement and graceful degradation: when budgets expire, the runtime should either return a structured partial result or fall back to a cheaper model variant, according to policy.
4) Maintain low friction for incremental adoption: defaults in SDKs and backward-compatible streaming frames.

Non-goals:
- Full redesign of the streaming protocol. We will iterate by adding optional frames and headers rather than replacing existing primitives.
- Heavyweight tracing library requirements on customers — the telemetry surface must be intentionally tiny.

User stories:
- As a frontend engineer, I want the SDK to automatically surface a partial answer when a downstream tool exceeds its budget so the user sees useful content rather than a spinner.
- As an SRE, I need telemetry that ties token generation latency to specific tool calls and SDK retries so incidents can be triaged quickly.
- As an SDK consumer, I want a straightforward knob to prefer lower-latency responses (possibly lower fidelity) without changing my prompt or model selection.

Requirements (functional):
- API surface: Add an optional per-request header/body field "latency_budget_ms" (integer) and an optional "tool_timeout_policy" enum (fail-fast | return-partial | degrade-model).
- Streaming frames: Introduce two optional frame types: TOOL_CALL_START and TOOL_CALL_RESULT. TOOL_CALL_START includes a short id, the declared expected tool_timeout_ms, and a compact call signature. TOOL_CALL_RESULT references the id and includes status (ok | error | timed_out) and a small, typed payload when available.
- SDK semantics: SDKs (JS/Python/Go) must: honor "latency_budget_ms" as a global cap for the request; track budget consumption, propagate budget to nested tool calls, and surface consistent partial-result callbacks. Default SDK policy: tool_timeout_policy=return-partial.
- Server behavior: If the cumulative time for generation + tool calls exceeds latency_budget_ms, server will follow the requested tool_timeout_policy. If not specified, server uses configuration: prioritize return-partial then fallback to degrade-model.

Requirements (non-functional):
- Telemetry payloads added to logs must be <1KB per request on average.
- Latency enforcement must add <2ms median overhead in the runtime for requests with 0 tool calls.
- Backwards compatibility: clients not supplying new headers/frames should continue to work unchanged.

SDK ergonomics guidance (principles):
- Opt-in explicitness: expose a small number of high-value knobs (latencyBudgetMs, toolTimeoutMs, fallbackPolicy) rather than many low-level flags.
- Simple async primitives: streaming callback, onPartialResult(partial), onToolPending(toolMetadata), onToolResult(id, result), onComplete(final), onError(error).
- Developer mental model: SDK docs should present the request lifecycle as: generation -> tool handshake -> tool execution -> finalization. Each step has a local budget and a global budget.
- Comfortable defaults: for web clients default latencyBudgetMs=1500ms, toolTimeoutMs=500ms, fallbackPolicy=return-partial. Mobile defaults prioritize lower latencies (latencyBudgetMs=900ms).

Telemetry design (compact schema):
- Fields (flat list): request_id, timestamp_ms, phase (generation|tool_start|tool_end|fallback), token_count_so_far, cumulative_latency_ms, tool_id (optional), tool_status (optional), cost_tokens, sdk_language, client_region.
- Emission points: SDK emits client-side telemetry at tool_start and tool_end; server emits server-side phases for generation and finalization. A consistent request_id joins the traces.
- Privacy: telemetry must avoid prompt/text contents by default — only token counts and aggregated cost metrics are emitted. If customers opt-in to richer traces for debug, warn and gate via account-level setting.

API examples (sketch):
- Request: POST /v1/generate with body fields {"prompt": "...", "latency_budget_ms": 1000, "tool_timeout_policy": "return-partial"} and streaming frames include: 
  -> TOOL_CALL_START {id: "t-1", expected_ms: 300, sig: "calendar.find(…)"}
  -> TOOL_CALL_RESULT {id: "t-1", status: "timed_out"}
  -> partial generation frames containing a structured placeholder {"tool_results": [{"id":"t-1","status":"timed_out"}], "text": "Found 2 possible slots. (partial)"}

Rollout plan and compatibility:
- Phase 0 (experiment): implement server-side frame handling and server telemetry, opt-in SDK flags in js-sdk experimental channel. Collect opt-in telemetry from internal pilots.
- Phase 1 (beta): default SDKs surface ergonomics and defaults; add admin account flags for richer tracing; provide migration guide.
- Phase 2 (GA): stable API header names, telemetry minimal guarantees, default handoff semantics.

Metrics and success criteria:
- Customer-observable: reduction in incidents where clients report indefinite streaming spinners due to tool calls by 60% in pilot accounts.
- Instrumentation: 95th percentile time to first partial result <= latencyBudgetMs for 90% of requests in web default config.
- Observability: ability to attribute 90% of token-level latency variance to one of (generation, tool execution, network, SDK) for requests with tool calls.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Should server preemptively hedge tool calls by invoking cheaper approximate tool variants? (cost vs complexity)
- How fine-grained should SDK telemetry be for debug mode without burdening customers with high cardinality logs?
- Should we expose a declarative policy language for handoffs (e.g., prefer-model-variant if tool latency > X) or keep it simple enums + server config?

Dependencies:
- SDK teams (JS/Python/Go) to add new callback primitives and default configs.
- Runtime infra to add low-overhead frame parsing and latency enforcement hooks.
- Console/observability to accept the compact telemetry schema and add join keys for request_id.

Next steps:
- Proto: engineering spike to implement TOOL_CALL_START/RESULT frames and measure overhead (1 week).
- SDK: experimental channel change in js-sdk to expose latencyBudgetMs and callbacks (2 weeks).
- Playground: create an interactive tutorial demonstrating partial-result flows and telemetry linking (3 weeks).

Appendix: example developer guidance (short):
- If you want faster UX for web chat: set latencyBudgetMs=1200 and fallbackPolicy=return-partial. Expect some tool results to be missing in partial mode; SDK will provide placeholders and onToolPending events.
- For high-reliability backend: set latencyBudgetMs to a larger value and fallbackPolicy=degrade-model so the platform can substitute a cheaper local model rather than returning partials.

Notes: This doc intentionally focuses on the intersection of SDK ergonomics and observability rather than deep protocol changes. It is a sketch intended to start engineering spike conversations and surface operational constraints.
